# Extension telemetry
An extension can report a few attributes about its own run. The CLI adds them to the
`command_invocation` event it already sends for that run. This page is the contract for
extension authors.

## How it works

When telemetry is on and the CLI has a registered schema for the extension, the CLI opens a
Unix socket and puts its path in the `CIRCLE_TELEMETRY_SOCKET` environment variable. The
extension connects to that socket, writes one JSON payload and closes the connection. The
CLI reads the payload after the extension exits and adds the attributes it accepts to the
event.

When the variable is not set, the extension reports nothing and must still work. It is not
set when telemetry is off, and when the extension has no registered schema. Never treat a
missing variable, or a failed write, as an error.

## Payload

The payload is one JSON object:

```json
{"version":1,"attributes":{"suggestions":0,"no_suggestion_reason":"saving_too_small"}}
```

* `version` is the integer 1. Any other value rejects the whole payload.
* `attributes` maps each short attribute name to its value.
* A value is a whole number, a boolean or one of the enum strings the schema lists for
  that attribute. A number must not be negative and must be within the schema bounds.
  A value that fails its check is dropped.

## Limits

* At most 20 attributes. This counts every attribute in the payload, including unknown names.
* At most 8 KB for the whole payload.
* An attribute name matches `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}$`.
* The CLI waits for the payload for a short time after the extension exits: 1 second at
  most. An extension that keeps the connection open, or sends nothing, does not hold up the CLI.

A payload over a limit is dropped as a whole. The CLI never changes its output or its exit
code because of a payload.

## Adding attributes

The CLI decides which attributes it accepts, so the CLI changes first and the extension
ships second.

1. Send a change to the schema in `internal/extschema/schema.go` in the circleci-cli
   repository. Add an entry to the extension's `attrs` list with its short name, its
   property name (it starts with `ext_`), its kind (int, enum or bool) and the bounds or
   the allowed values. Add the extension to `specs` if it has no schema yet. Then
   refresh `internal/extschema/schema.json` with `task test -- ./internal/extschema/... -update`.
2. Release the CLI.
3. Ship the extension version that reports the attribute.

An attribute that is not in the CLI's schema is dropped, so an extension that ships first
loses its data until the CLI catches up.

## Status

Every extension run sets `extension_attributes_status` on the event, so you can see
what became of the payload.

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `accepted` | The payload was valid and every attribute in it was accepted. This includes an empty `attributes` object |
| `partially_accepted` | Some attributes were accepted and some were dropped |
| `rejected` | The payload was read, but nothing was accepted: an unsupported `version`, more than 20 attributes, or no valid attribute |
| `not_supported` | The extension has no registered schema, or it never connected to the socket |
| `no_payload` | The extension connected and closed without sending data |
| `read_failed` | The payload could not be read: invalid JSON, over 8 KB, a broken connection, or no data within the wait |
| `setup_failed` | The CLI could not open the socket, so the extension ran without the variable |

The event also carries `extension_version`, the installed version of the extension. The
CLI sends it only when it is a valid semantic version with three numbers, such as `1.2.3` or
`1.2.3-rc.1`, and omits it otherwise.
